title: Docker basics
summary: Package your AI app and all its dependencies into a portable container that runs the same on any machine.
objectives: Explain what a container is and why "works on my machine" stops being a problem
Tell the difference between an image and a container
Write a simple Dockerfile for a Python AI app
Build an image and run it as a container with docker build and docker run
Pass secrets like ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in safely with environment variables
Map ports so you can reach a running app from your browser
Use .dockerignore and a requirements.txt for clean, reproducible builds

quiz.q: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
quiz.answer: An image is the read-only blueprint (built once); a container is a running instance of that image.
quiz.why: Like a class versus an object: you build one image, then run many containers from it.

quiz.q: Which command builds an image from a Dockerfile in the current folder and tags it 'myapp'?
quiz.why: docker build reads the Dockerfile, -t myapp names the image, and the dot is the build context (current folder).

quiz.q: Why should you NOT hard-code your ANTHROPIC_API_KEY inside the Dockerfile?
quiz.answer: Anyone with the image could read the key; pass it at runtime with -e or --env-file instead.
quiz.why: Image layers are inspectable, so baked-in secrets leak. Inject them at run time and keep them in env vars.

quiz.q: In 'docker run -p 8000:80 myapp', what does 8000:80 mean?
options: Host port 8000 maps to container port 80
Container port 8000 maps to host port 80
quiz.why: The format is host:container — traffic to localhost:8000 is forwarded to port 80 inside the container.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a .dockerignore file?
quiz.answer: It lists files and folders to exclude from the build context, so secrets and junk like .env or venv are not copied in.
quiz.why: Smaller, cleaner builds and no accidental leaking of local files or credentials into the image.

quiz.q: True or false — a container automatically keeps all its files after you delete and re-run it.
quiz.why: False. Containers are ephemeral; data written inside is lost unless you use a volume or bind mount to persist it.

body_markdown:
## Why Docker?

You have built an A I app that runs on your laptop. But "it works on my machine" is not a deployment plan. The server might have a different Python version, missing libraries, or different settings. **Docker** solves this by packaging your code *and* everything it needs — Python, libraries, files — into a single portable unit called a **container** that runs the same everywhere.

Think of a container as a sealed lunchbox: whatever you put in stays exactly as packed, no matter whose fridge it ends up in.

## Images vs containers

This is the one distinction to nail. An **image** is the read-only blueprint — built once, stored on disk. A **container** is a running instance of that image. One image, many containers, like a class and its objects in code.

```bash
docker build -t myapp .     # build the image (blueprint)
docker run myapp            # start a container from it
docker ps                   # list running containers
```

## Writing a Dockerfile

A **Dockerfile** is a recipe: each line is a step Docker runs to build your image. Start from an official base image, copy your code in, install dependencies, then say how to start.

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
```

Copying `requirements.txt` *before* the rest of your code lets Docker cache the slow `pip install` step, so rebuilds are fast when only your code changes.

## Secrets and the Anthropic API

Never bake an API key into the image — anyone who pulls it can read the layers. Keep keys in **environment variables** and pass them in at run time. Your code reads the key from the environment; Docker hands it over with `-e` or `--env-file`.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello from inside a container!"}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

Then run it without ever writing the key into a file the image keeps:

```bash
docker run -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY myapp
```

## Ports and persistence

If your app serves a web page or A P I, you must **map a port** so your browser can reach inside the container. The format is `host:container`. Also remember containers are **ephemeral**: files written inside vanish when the container is removed, unless you mount a **volume**.

```bash
docker run -p 8000:80 myapp        # localhost:8000 -> port 80 inside
docker run -v $(pwd)/data:/app/data myapp
```

## Your task

Take the A I app you built earlier and write a Dockerfile for it. Add a `.dockerignore` (exclude `.env`, `venv`, `__pycache__`), build the image, and run it — passing your `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` as an environment variable.

slides.title: Why Docker?
bullets: "Works on my machine" is not a deployment plan.
Servers differ: Python version, libraries, settings.
Docker packages code plus everything it needs.
Same behaviour everywhere it runs.
slides.narration: So why do we even need Docker? Your app runs fine on your laptop, but the server might have a different Python version or be missing a library. Docker fixes this by wrapping your code and all its dependencies into one sealed unit. Think of it as a lunchbox: whatever you pack stays exactly as packed, no matter whose fridge it lands in.

slides.title: Images vs containers
bullets: An image is the read-only blueprint.
A container is a running instance of it.
One image can run many containers.
Like a class and its objects.
slides.narration: Here's the one distinction you must nail. An image is the blueprint, built once and stored on disk. A container is a running instance of that image. From a single image you can launch many containers, just like creating many objects from one class in your code. Keep that picture in mind and the rest follows.

slides.title: The Dockerfile recipe
bullets: A Dockerfile is a list of build steps.
Start FROM an official base image.
COPY code in, RUN to install, CMD to start.
slides.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
slides.narration: A Dockerfile is just a recipe. Each line is a step Docker runs to build your image. We start FROM an official Python base image, set a working folder, copy in our requirements, install them, copy the rest of our code, and finally say which command starts the app. Notice we copy requirements first, so Docker can cache the slow install step.

slides.title: Build and run
bullets: docker build makes the image.
The dot is the build context, the current folder.
docker run starts a container.
docker ps lists what's running.
slides.code:
docker build -t myapp .
docker run myapp
docker ps
slides.narration: Two commands do the heavy lifting. Docker build reads your Dockerfile and creates the image; the dash t names it myapp, and the dot tells Docker to use the current folder as the build context. Docker run then starts a container from that image. And docker p s shows you everything currently running.

slides.title: Keep secrets safe
bullets: Never bake API keys into the image.
Image layers can be read by anyone.
Pass keys at run time with -e.
Your code reads them from the environment.
slides.narration: Big rule: never hard-code your A P I key inside the Dockerfile. Image layers can be inspected, so a baked-in secret leaks to anyone who pulls the image. Instead, keep the key in an environment variable and pass it in at run time with dash e. Your Python code reads it from the environment, so the image itself never holds the secret.

slides.title: Calling Claude inside
bullets: The Anthropic client reads the key from env.
Same code, now portable in a container.
Use a current model id.
slides.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()
msg = client.messages.create(
  model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
  max_tokens=1024,
  messages=[{"role":"user",
             "content":"Hi!"}])
slides.narration: Here's the app code running inside the container. We create the Anthropic client, which automatically reads the A P I key from the environment we passed in. Then we call messages dot create with a current model id, claude sonnet four dash six, and a max tokens limit. Same code as before, but now fully portable.

slides.title: Ports and persistence
bullets: Map a port so the browser can reach in.
Format is host colon container.
Containers are ephemeral by default.
Use a volume to keep data.
slides.code:
docker run -p 8000:80 myapp
docker run \
  -v $(pwd)/data:/app/data myapp
slides.narration: If your app serves a web page, you must map a port so your browser can reach inside the container. The format is host port colon container port, so localhost eight thousand reaches port eighty inside. And remember: containers are ephemeral. Anything written inside disappears when the container is removed, unless you mount a volume to persist it.

slides.title: Clean builds
bullets: List dependencies in requirements.txt.
Add a .dockerignore file.
Exclude .env, venv, __pycache__.
Smaller images, no leaked secrets.
slides.narration: Two small habits make builds clean and safe. First, pin your dependencies in a requirements dot t x t file so installs are reproducible. Second, add a dot dockerignore file that excludes things like your dot e n v secrets, your virtual environment, and cache folders. This keeps your image small and stops local secrets from sneaking in.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Confusing an image with a container.
Baking secrets into the Dockerfile.
Forgetting to map a port with -p.
Expecting container files to persist.
slides.narration: Let's flag the slip-ups that catch most beginners. One: confusing the image, the blueprint, with the container, the running instance. Two: baking secrets into the Dockerfile instead of passing them at run time. Three: forgetting dash p, so your app runs but you can't reach it. And four: expecting files inside a container to stick around. Watch for these four and you'll save real time.
